title: Who doesn't fast
hookLine: the ill, travelers, pregnant and nursing women, the elderly, and menstruating women

lines: TRAVELERS ON THE ROAD IN RAMADAN.
cards: Travelers on the road in Ramadan with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Some are fasting. Some are eating.
They ride together, stop together, and, the report says, nobody blames anybody: the fasting don't look down on the eating, and the eating don't look down on the fasting.
It's a small scene, told by his companion Anas, and it shows a softer side of the pillar. The fast has an exit door built into the very verses that command it.

teach.b: The word is rukhsah: a concession, an allowance Allah has made. First, it sits right next to the command.
Surah two, in Pickthall's words: "and (for) him who is sick among you, or on a journey, (the same) number of other days." The sick and the traveler may leave the fast and keep it another time.
The next verse says why: "Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you." Second, the list grows.
A report in the Sunan of Abu Dawud and others says Allah has lifted the fast from the traveler, and from the pregnant and the nursing woman.

Scholars also excuse someone too old or frail to fast at all; a later day comes back to what they do instead. And a woman during her period does not fast; the legal books treat the bleeding after childbirth the same way.

Aisha, the Prophet's wife, said in a report in Sahih Muslim that they were told to make up missed fasts but not missed prayers. For her it isn't a concession to choose; it's a time the fast doesn't apply.
Third, taking the allowance is not a lesser path. A report in the Musnad of Ahmad has the Prophet ﷺ say that Allah loves for his concessions to be taken.
Scholars discuss when a traveler should fast and when an illness is serious enough, but the principle is plain: hardship that harms is not what the fast is for.

teach.h: HE DESIRETH NOT HARDSHIP FOR YOU.
teach.b: Nobody judges. For anyone keeping a practice next to someone who, today, isn't: the reasons may be invisible, and in this teaching, they're between that person and Allah.

how: Muslims who are ill, traveling, pregnant, nursing or elderly may leave the Ramadan fast, and women do not fast during menstruation or after childbirth; the days are made up later by those who can, and those who never can feed a poor person instead.

o: an allowance not to fast, for illness, travel and more
a fine paid for each fasting day a person misses
a shortened fast that ends early in the afternoon

games.q: who doesn't fast — tap the pairs.
p: the same number of other days

s: taking the allowance not to fast is a lesser kind of faith
a report in Ahmad says Allah loves for his concessions to be taken.
the Qur'an's verses on the fast name the sick and the traveler
"him who is sick among you, or on a journey, (the same) number of other days" (2:184).
on the road with the Prophet, the fasting criticized the ones who ate
Anas says nobody blamed anybody, either way.

games.q: you're on the road in Ramadan with the Prophet ﷺ. some of your companions are fasting, and some are eating. what does Anas say happened?
o: the fasting ones scolded the eaters.
the eaters were sent to ride separately.
games.why: nobody blamed anybody. the fasting didn't fault the eaters, and the eaters didn't fault the fasting.

practice: Run slowly through the list, the sick, the traveler, the pregnant, the nursing, the elderly, the woman in her period, and let a face come to mind for one of them.
Then turn to yourself: is there a rule you keep, about work, food, exercise, anything, even when it hurts you? Just notice it, and if you pray, ask Allah for ease.

wordCard.voice: Rukhsah. A concession: the permission not to fast when illness, travel, pregnancy, nursing, age or a woman's period make it a hardship. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a concession or allowance; in law, a permission that eases a rule for those in hardship.

carryVoice: Your line: the fast bends. Ease is part of the command. Until tomorrow.
